segments.title: Pictures give readers a reference for imagining the past
segments.summary: Pictures give readers a visual reference for imagining the people, places, objects, and events described in historical prose.
segments.body: Historical prose often asks readers to imagine people, places, objects, and events they have never seen. Pictures give that imagination a visual reference and help set it in motion. An unillustrated work may feel like a serious historical tome with a smaller audience. A well-chosen image can make the text more inviting while leaving the historian's explanation central.

evidence.note: He explains that pictures ignite imagination and provide a reference for it.

segments.title: How many pictures can a historical text carry?
segments.summary: Journal articles leave little room for illustrations, while heavily illustrated books may encourage readers to skim the pictures and overlook the text.
segments.body: Journal articles usually leave little room for pictures, so authors cannot illustrate every point. Books allow more freedom, but too many images can turn a work into a large, heavy picture book. Readers may enjoy the illustrations while treating the historical argument as secondary. The warning comes from friends who produced well-received books yet felt that hardly anyone had read the text. Illustrations work best when they support the writing without overwhelming it.

evidence.note: He contrasts journal space limits with the risk of an over-illustrated book making the text secondary.

segments.title: A practical ratio of one picture per thousand words
segments.summary: A working rule of thumb is roughly one picture per thousand words, which would give a 45,000-word primer about 45 images.
segments.body: A working rule of thumb is one image for every thousand words. Applied to a planned series of 45,000-word primers, that gives each book about 45 pictures. This is a personal publishing judgement, not a universal rule. The aim is to include enough illustration to make the book appealing while keeping the text central.

evidence.note: He states his one-picture-per-thousand-words rule and applies it to 45,000-word primers.

segments.title: Image rights shape the cost of history books
segments.summary: Licensing images from museums and archives can make a history book substantially more expensive than a work of fiction of the same length.
segments.body: Historical illustrations add a cost that a comparable work of fiction may avoid. Museums and archives rely on access rights as an important revenue source, so authors often have to budget for licensed photographs. Personal photographs or images supplied by friends can cover part of the requirement, although some rights may still need to be purchased. Fiction publishers may pay for cover art and editorial work without also buying historical-photo rights. A single photograph can cost as much as £1,000.

evidence.note: He describes museum and archive image rights, personal photo sources, and a possible one-thousand-pound charge for one historical photo.
